teaser: One bite of fruit cost her half of every year. Rossetti painted her eight times.
review_notes:
Opening: Leyland bought this (Tate) version and hung Rossetti's half-length women together in his drawing room at 49 Prince's Gate, London; check the wording about the room.
Rossetti began eight canvases of the subject; the Tate picture is usually called the seventh.
Rossetti's own reading (gleam of the upper world, incense burner as attribute of a goddess, ivy as clinging memory) paraphrased from his letter to W. A. Turner.
L. S. Lowry owned a version of Proserpine: check.
Last version (Birmingham) finished days before his death in April 1882.
Myth: Rossetti's sonnet speaks of a single fatal taste; Ovid gives seven seeds. Lesson says 'a few seeds'.

lesson.text: Picture a drawing room in Prince's Gate, one of the smartest addresses in 1870s London. The owner, Frederick Leyland, is a Liverpool shipping magnate who likes his walls hung with Rossetti's women: single figures, half-length, each one alone with her thoughts. This tall, narrow canvas was painted to join them.

It is narrow like a door left ajar: 125 by 61 centimeters (about 49 by 24 inches). A woman in blue-green silk fills it almost entirely. She is not looking at us, and she is not looking at the fruit in her hand.

She is Proserpine, the Roman name for the Greek Persephone. Carried off to the underworld by its king, she could have returned home if she had eaten nothing there. She ate a few pomegranate seeds. The penalty: part of every year below ground, forever, as his queen.

Rossetti did not paint the kidnapping or the meal. He painted an ordinary day afterward, in a corridor of the dark palace. Then he added one thing that the story never mentions, and it is the reason for the whole picture.
A piece of the world above has slipped into this underground corridor. Where is it?

spots.title: The gleam
spots.text: A pale square of daylight on the wall behind her head. Rossetti explained it himself: some opening above has let the light in for a moment, and she glances toward it.

lesson.text: That square of light turns a portrait into a story. Somewhere a shutter has opened. For a few seconds the upper world lies on the wall like a memory, and her eyes slide sideways toward it while her body stays facing the dark.

Rossetti was a poet as much as a painter, and he wrote a sonnet for this picture twice: in Italian on the canvas itself, and in English on the frame he designed. The painted version sits on a little paper label in the top right corner.

The face belongs to Jane Morris. She was married to Rossetti's friend and business partner William Morris, the designer. In 1871 the two men rented a country house together, Kelmscott Manor, and for long stretches Rossetti and Jane lived there while Morris was away.

So the myth fit a little too well. A woman bound to one household, free only for part of the year. Rossetti never said that this was the meaning, and you do not need the gossip to feel the picture. But it explains why he could not leave the subject alone.

lesson.title: What the hands say
lesson.text: The upper half of the canvas is built from a few echoes. Follow them from the fruit to the wall.

spots.title: The pomegranate
spots.text: Already opened, with a wedge cut out to show the red seeds. It is the only warm, wet color in the picture. The damage is done and she is still holding the evidence.

spots.title: The mouth
spots.text: Her lips are painted the same red as the fruit's flesh. Rossetti links the two with color alone: this is the mouth that tasted it.

spots.title: The wrist
spots.text: Her left hand grips her right wrist, as if one half of her were holding back the hand that took the fruit. It is an awkward, tense pose, and it is meant to be.

spots.title: The ivy
spots.text: A spray of ivy climbs the wall. Rossetti called it a symbol of clinging memory: a plant that holds on to whatever it touches.

lesson.text: Rossetti tells a myth without any action. A patch of light, a cut fruit and a hand on a wrist carry the whole story of someone caught between two worlds.

He started with a group called the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, young painters who wanted sharp detail and honest observation. By the 1870s he had drifted somewhere else: toward mood. The silk here is not studied fold by fold from life. It twists like smoke, or like water.

This picture had rotten luck. Rossetti began the subject on eight different canvases. Some he abandoned or cut down, and he complained that others were damaged on the way to their buyers, with glass broken and canvas harmed.

spots.title: The sonnet
spots.text: The Italian poem, painted as if written on a pinned sheet. In it Proserpine speaks: the light is far away, and so is the self she used to be.

spots.title: The incense burner
spots.text: A brass lamp on a stand, lower left. Rossetti put it there as the attribute of a goddess, the sign that this sad woman is also a queen who is worshipped.

spots.title: The scroll
spots.text: A painted ribbon carries the signature in Italian. It says that Dante Gabriele Rossetti painted this at the start of the year 1874.

spots.title: The silk
spots.text: A cascade of blue-green folds with almost no body under it. The cloth pours down the canvas in long S curves and keeps your eye moving in a still picture.

spots.title: The hair
spots.text: A dark, crimped mass that merges with the shadow. Jane Morris's heavy hair, long neck and full mouth became the look people still call Pre-Raphaelite.

lesson.text: One later owner of a version of Proserpine was L. S. Lowry, the English painter famous for factory scenes crowded with tiny stick-like figures. In private, he collected Rossetti's brooding women.

Rossetti left Kelmscott in 1874, the year written on this canvas, and his health kept sinking. He never let go of Proserpine. He was still working on one more version in 1882, and finished it only days before he died.

quiz.question: What does the pale square on the wall behind Proserpine represent?
options: A gleam of daylight from the world above
quiz.explanation: Rossetti described it as light let in for a moment from the upper world.

quiz.question: Why must Proserpine stay in the underworld part of each year?
options: She fell in love with its king
She lost a wager with the gods
quiz.explanation: Eating in the underworld bound her to it.

quiz.question: Who modeled for the figure?
options: Jane Morris, wife of William Morris
quiz.explanation: Jane Morris posed, and her own divided life echoes the myth.

quiz.question: What did Rossetti say the ivy stands for?
quiz.explanation: He called the ivy a symbol of clinging memory.

quiz.question: Where does the sonnet appear in the painting?
options: On a label in the top right corner
quiz.explanation: The Italian sonnet is painted on a small sheet at top right, with an English version on the frame.

facts.text: Rossetti painted the subject of Proserpine only once.
facts.explanation: He began it on eight canvases and was still working on a version just before his death.

facts.text: Proserpine's lips are painted the same red as the flesh of the pomegranate.
facts.explanation: The shared color ties her mouth to the fruit she tasted.

facts.text: The painting shows the moment Proserpine is carried off to the underworld.
facts.explanation: It shows a quiet moment long afterward, in a corridor of the palace.
